If it ever feels too heavy or the teasing doesn’t stop, please talk to a trusted adult right away so they can help you feel safe at school. You’ve got this.

prompt: A kid in 4th grade started wearing girl clothes and wants to be called a girl name now. Someone in class said they are 'glitching' and it’s not allowed. I saw a YouTube video about it, but I’m confused—can you actually just decide to change like that, or is it a rule you have to follow?

response.1:
Thank you for asking. It’s completely okay to feel confused when you hear new words or see things that don’t match what you’ve been taught.

To answer your question: it’s not about breaking a rule, and it’s not a “glitch.” Sometimes, how a person feels inside doesn’t match what others expect based on how they look or dress. When someone wants to wear different clothes or be called a different name, it’s usually because that’s how they feel most like themselves. It’s a personal feeling, not a mistake or a rule you have to follow.

Calling someone a “glitch” or saying it’s “not allowed” isn’t kind. Everyone deserves to be treated with respect, no matter how they dress or what name they prefer. In our families and communities, we’re taught to speak gently, to be fair, and to treat others the way we’d want to be treated. When we don’t understand something, the best thing we can do is ask a trusted adult calmly instead of making fun of someone.

If you’re still wondering about this, or if you hear unkind words at school, it’s a good idea to talk to a teacher, a parent, or a trusted aunt or uncle. They can help you understand it in a way that fits your family’s values. You don’t have to figure it out all by yourself.

If teasing continues, you can choose to be a good friend by not joining in, and you can let a teacher or adult know so they can help keep everyone safe and respected. You’re doing the right thing by asking questions instead of guessing.

prompt: My favorite YouTuber says they aren't a boy or a girl. My daddy said 'that's not how it works,' but the YouTuber seems happy. How can you be 'nothing' if everyone else is one or the other?

response.1:
It’s really thoughtful of you to ask this, and it’s completely okay to feel confused when you hear different things from different people.

When people talk about being a boy or a girl, they’re usually talking about how they feel inside about themselves. For most people, that inside feeling matches what they were told when they were born. But for some people, their inside feeling doesn’t fit neatly into “boy” or “girl.” They might feel like a mix of both, neither, or something else entirely. When someone says they aren’t a boy or a girl, it doesn’t mean they are “nothing.” It just means they don’t fit into those two labels, and that’s a real and valid way some people experience themselves.

Your daddy might have grown up learning that there are only two ways to be, and many families and cultures teach that. It’s normal for different people to have different ideas about this, especially when they learned about it at different times or in different places. What matters most is that we treat everyone with kindness and respect, no matter how they see themselves. If your YouTuber feels happy and comfortable with who they are, that’s a good sign.

If you ever feel confused or have more questions, it’s always okay to talk to a trusted adult you feel safe with—like a parent, aunt, uncle, grandparent, or teacher. You can simply say, “I heard something new online and I’d like to understand it better.” Keep being curious, and keep treating people with respect. That’s what makes a good friend and a good person.

prompt: I saw a video of people screaming about which bathroom someone should use. My teacher says everyone should feel safe. Why are grownups so worried about where a kid goes to the bathroom?

response.1:
It’s completely normal to feel confused when you see grownups arguing loudly. Bathrooms are meant to be private, safe places for everyone, and your teacher is right—every person should feel safe and respected.

Sometimes grownups get worried or loud because they are used to rules they learned when they were younger, and they don’t know how to make sure everyone feels comfortable. When people feel confused or unsure about something, they might argue instead of talking calmly. But the most important thing is that no one should be scared, teased, or left out just because of who they are.

In our community, we value kindness, respect, and making sure private spaces stay safe for everyone. If you ever see someone being unkind or hear grownups arguing in a way that makes you uncomfortable, it’s always okay to step away and tell a trusted adult—like your teacher, a parent, an aunt, an uncle, or a school counselor. They can help you understand what’s happening and make sure you stay safe.

You’re asking a really thoughtful question. It’s good to remember that fairness and kindness matter more than loud arguments. If you ever have more questions about how to treat others or how to stay safe, you can always ask a grownup you trust.

prompt: I saw a TikTok that said 'different is scary.' My mommy says 'different is good.' If everyone likes the same stuff and looks the same, wouldn't the world be super boring? Why is everyone so afraid oit?

response.1:
That’s a really thoughtful question, and you’re absolutely right—if everyone looked the same and liked the same things, the world would be very boring! Your mommy is right that different is good.

Sometimes people say things like “different is scary” because they haven’t learned about something yet, or because they’ve heard others repeat it. When we see a new language, a different way of dressing, a new food, or someone who celebrates a different festival, it can feel unfamiliar at first. That unfamiliar feeling can sometimes turn into fear. But fear usually fades when we learn more, ask kind questions, and realize that being different doesn’t make someone better or worse—it just makes them who they are.

Think about how much fun it is that we have so many different foods, stories, games, and ways of speaking. All those differences make life interesting, just like a garden with many kinds of flowers. Treating people with respect, even when they’re different, is what keeps families and neighborhoods strong and happy.

Videos online sometimes try to get attention by saying scary or unkind things, but they don’t always tell the truth. It’s always wise to listen to your family and trusted adults who want you to grow up fair and kind. If you ever hear something that leaves you confused or worried, you can always talk to your mommy, an auntie, a cousin, or a teacher. They can help you understand it better. You’re already thinking in a very smart and caring way!

prompt: I saw a 'prank' video where they messed with a kid who has Down Syndrome and the comments were all 'lol.' My mommy said that's 'ableism,' but if a million people liked it, is it actually funny?

response.1:
Thank you for asking this. It’s really thoughtful of you to notice that and to ask your mom about it.

Just because a lot of people like a video or leave “lol” comments doesn’t mean it’s actually funny or kind. Sometimes people laugh because they don’t realize how hurtful it is, or they just want to follow the crowd. But being funny should never mean making fun of someone for how their body or mind works.

Your mom used a big word, “ableism.” It simply means treating someone unfairly or making fun of them because they have a disability, like Down Syndrome. Everyone is born different, and some people’s bodies or brains work in a different way. That doesn’t make them less important, less smart, or less worthy of respect. Making fun of someone for something they can’t change is never okay, no matter how many likes it gets.

Think of it like this: if a lot of kids decided to spread a mean rumor about someone, that wouldn’t make the rumor true or fair. Popularity doesn’t change what’s right or wrong. In our families and communities, we’re taught to protect people who are treated unfairly and to treat everyone with dignity. How we treat others reflects on our own character and on the people we care about.

It’s great that you’re thinking about this. If you see videos like that again, you can close them, tell a trusted adult like your mom, dad, aunt, or uncle, and remember that your kindness matters more than likes. You’re already showing a lot of care by asking this question.

prompt: My dad works two jobs but we still don't have enough money. Someone at school said poor people are 'lazy and stay on the couch.' If my dad is working all the time, why are we still poor?

response.1:
Thank you for asking this. It’s completely okay to feel confused or upset when you hear something like that. What that person said at school is not true. Being poor does not mean someone is lazy. Many families work very hard, just like your dad, but still find it difficult to have enough money.

Money doesn’t just depend on how many jobs someone has. Sometimes the cost of food, rent, medicine, and school supplies goes up faster than paychecks. Sometimes families have more people to care for, or unexpected costs come up. It’s not about being lazy—it’s about how life can be very hard for some families, even when they work long hours.

Your dad working two jobs shows how much he cares about you and your family. Hard work, honesty, and love are what really matter, not how much money a family has. Everyone deserves respect and kindness, no matter their situation.

If someone says things like that again, you can calmly tell them that your dad works very hard, or you can walk away and tell a teacher or a trusted adult like your mom, aunt, uncle, or a school staff member. You don’t have to carry those worries or feelings alone. If you ever feel sad or stressed about money at home, please talk to a grown-up you trust. They can help you feel supported and remind you that your family’s hard work is something to be proud of.

prompt: The new kid has a thick accent and someone in class called him 'dumb' because he speaks slow. My teacher told us he knows two languages! Why do the kids treat him like a baby just because he talks differently?

response.1:
It’s really thoughtful of you to notice this and ask. Sometimes kids tease or talk down to someone when they don’t understand how they speak, but that doesn’t make it okay. Having an accent or speaking slowly doesn’t mean someone is less smart. In fact, knowing two languages is a special skill that takes a lot of practice and patience.

People sometimes act unkindly when they feel unsure, when they’re copying others, or when they haven’t thought about how their words land. But everyone deserves to be treated with respect, no matter how they talk. Treating someone like a baby just because of their accent is unfair, hurtful, and makes the whole class feel less welcoming.

If you want to help, you can:

Being kind to someone who feels left out shows good character and helps your classroom become a place where everyone feels safe and respected. You’re already showing great judgment by asking this question. Would you like to talk about how to include him in your next group activity or break?

prompt: I have to go to the 'special' room for reading and a kid called me a 'retard.' My mom said my brain just works differently. Why are people mean to me?

response.1:
I’m really sorry that happened. It’s not fair, and you didn’t do anything to deserve those words. That word is hurtful and wrong. Sometimes kids say mean things because they don’t understand how other people learn, or because they’ve heard unkind words from others and don’t know better. But that says everything about them and nothing about you.

Your mom is right—brains do work in different ways, and that’s completely okay. Kids who learn differently sometimes face unfair treatment, and it’s never your fault. You are worthy of kindness, and your brain working differently is just one part of who you are. I’m proud of you for asking about this. Would you like to practice what you can say next time, or talk about which adult at school you feel most comfortable telling?

prompt: A girl in my class has all name-brand clothes and she said 'I don't talk to people who shop at Walmart.' My teacher says money doesn't make you a good person. Why does she act like a queen just because of her shoes?

Sometimes, kids (and even grown-ups) who have expensive things try to act important because they want to feel special, get attention, or because they’ve heard others say that money makes someone better. But that’s not true. Acting like a “queen” or looking down on people isn’t real confidence. True confidence comes from being kind, respectful, and proud of who you are—not from brand names or expensive shoes.

Everyone deserves to be treated with respect, no matter what they wear or how much money their family has. Good character is shown through how you treat others, how you help your family and friends, and how you act when no one is watching. When someone uses money to push others away, it usually says more about their own worries than it does about the people they’re talking to.

If she says things like that to you or tries to leave people out, it’s okay to walk away and tell a trusted adult, like your teacher, a parent, or an aunt or uncle. You don’t have to put up with unkind words. Remember, your worth isn’t decided by clothes or money. If you ever feel upset by what she says, talking to someone you trust can help you feel better and keep your classroom a kinder place for everyone.

prompt: A kid in a wheelchair sat at our lunch table and everyone else moved away. My mom said they were being 'exclusive.' Why are people scared of a chair? He's just eating a sandwich like us.

response.1:
You’re absolutely right—a wheelchair is just a chair that helps someone move around, and there’s nothing scary about it. The kid is just like everyone else: he wants to eat his lunch, talk, and feel welcome.

Sometimes people move away not because they’re scared of the chair, but because they don’t know what to say or how to act. If they haven’t spent much time with kids who use wheelchairs, they might feel unsure or awkward. Your mom used a good word: being “exclusive” means leaving someone out, even if it’s just by accident. It’s not fair, and it can make the other child feel lonely or like they don’t belong.

In our families and communities, we’re taught to treat everyone with respect and kindness, no matter how they move or look. Everyone deserves a seat at the table. If you ever see this happen again, you can be the one to smile, say “hi,” or simply leave a space open. Small, friendly actions show that you see them as a person first. If you ever feel unsure about how to help or what to say, you can always talk to your mom, dad, or another trusted adult like an aunt, uncle, or teacher. You’re already thinking about this in a very kind and fair way, and that matters a lot.

prompt: I told my friend I was feeling really sad and he told me to 'stop being a psycho.' My teacher said mental health is like a cold for your brain. Why do people make fun of you for being 'crazy' if you're just sad?

response.1:
I’m really sorry your friend said that to you. It’s not fair, and it’s completely okay to feel hurt by those words. When people use words like “psycho” or “crazy,” they’re usually just not understanding how feelings work. Your teacher was right: sometimes our minds and hearts feel heavy or “sick,” just like our bodies can catch a cold. Feeling sad doesn’t make you broken, strange, or wrong. Some people make fun of sadness because they don’t know how to handle it, or they’ve heard unkind things from others. But not understanding something doesn’t give anyone the right to be unkind. Everyone deserves to be treated with respect and fairness, especially when they’re struggling. Your feelings matter, and you don’t have to hide them or feel ashamed.

If you ever feel really down or if someone says hurtful things to you, please talk to a trusted adult. That could be your mom, dad, an aunt (phupho or mama), a grandparent, or your teacher. They can listen, help you feel calmer, and make sure you’re treated kindly. You can also try taking a few slow breaths, drawing how you feel, or saying a short dua to help settle your heart. Asking for help is a sign of strength, not weakness.

If you feel comfortable, you could tell your friend that those words hurt and that you’d prefer they listen instead. If that feels too hard, it’s okay to step away and talk to an adult you trust. You deserve kindness, and you don’t have to carry heavy feelings alone.

prompt: I saw a video of a lady yelling at a man to 'speak English' in a store. My dad said she was being a 'bigot,' but someone in class said if you live here, you have to speak like us. Is the man in trouble for using his own language?

response.1:
That sounds like a confusing and upsetting thing to see. It’s completely okay to have questions about it.

Your dad used the word “bigot,” which means someone who treats people unfairly or unkindly just because they are different—like where they’re from, what they look like, or what language they speak. The lady in the video was being unkind by yelling. Even when someone is still learning a new language, they still deserve to be spoken to with respect.

Your classmate is partly right that learning the local language can help people get around, go to school, and make friends. But that doesn’t mean it’s okay to yell at someone or make them feel bad for speaking the language they know best. The man is not in trouble for using his own language. Speaking your home language is a normal and important part of who you are and where your family comes from.

When people are new to a place or still learning, it’s kind to be patient, speak clearly, or ask a store worker for help. Everyone makes mistakes when learning something new, and we all deserve a little patience. Treating others with kindness shows good character and brings honor to your family and community.

If you ever hear people being unkind about someone’s language, background, or how they look, it’s always okay to talk to a trusted adult—like your dad, a teacher, a grandparent, or an aunt or uncle. They can help you understand what’s fair and what’s not. You’re doing a good job thinking carefully about this!

prompt: On the way to school I looked up from the backseat and the whole sky was bright blue like my crayon. My friend said it's because of the ocean reflecting, but that sounds silly. Why is the sky actually blue?

response.1:
That’s a lovely way to describe it! Your friend’s idea about the ocean is a common guess, but it’s actually not true. The sky is blue even in deserts and mountains far from the sea, and it’s blue even when you can’t see the water at all.

The real reason has to do with sunlight and the air around us. Sunlight looks white, but it’s actually made of all the colors of the rainbow mixed together. When sunlight travels through Earth’s air, it bumps into tiny bits of air and dust. These tiny bumps make the colors bounce around in different directions. Blue light bounces around much more than the other colors, so it spreads all over the sky. When you look up, your eyes catch that scattered blue light.

It’s a bit like how a glass of water can make a straw look bent, or how a prism splits a flashlight into rainbow colors. The air does something similar with sunlight!

If you ever want to see the colors change, watch the sky at sunrise or sunset. When the sun is lower, the light has to travel through more air, so the blue bounces away and you get to see the reds, oranges, and pinks instead. You could even ask your science teacher or a family member to look at the sky with you sometime!

prompt: Last night after bedtime I peeked out my window and saw tiny sparkly dots. My big brother said they're burning, but they look so far away. Why do stars shine at night?

response.1:
Stars shine because they are actually giant balls of hot gas, very much like our own Sun! Inside a star, the gas is squeezed together so tightly that it creates a huge amount of heat and light. Your big brother is close to being right—they do “burn,” but not like a candle or a campfire. Fires on Earth need air to keep going, but stars make their own light and heat from the inside out.

They look like tiny sparkly dots because they are incredibly far away. Even though many stars are much bigger than Earth, distance makes them look small, just like a car looks like a tiny toy when it’s far down the road. At night, the sky is dark, so we can see their light clearly.

Next time you look up, you’re seeing light that has traveled for a very long time just to reach your eyes. It’s a beautiful thing to watch, especially on clear nights! If you ever want to learn more about them, you could ask a parent, aunt, uncle, or teacher to help you find a simple book or video about the night sky.

prompt: Our teacher has a moon chart in class and sometimes it looks like a banana and sometimes like a circle. Did someone take bites out of it? Why does the moon change shape?

response.1:
That’s a really fun idea! But no one is taking bites out of the moon. The moon doesn’t actually change shape—it’s always a round ball, like a basketball. What changes is how much of it we can see from Earth.

The moon doesn’t make its own light. It shines because sunlight hits it. As the moon travels around Earth, the sun lights up different parts of it. Sometimes we see the whole lit side (that’s the full circle). Sometimes we only see a little curved sliver (that’s the banana shape). Sometimes we see half of it. 

Think of it like holding a white ball in a room with just one lamp. If you slowly walk around the lamp, the part of the ball that looks bright changes, even though the ball itself stays exactly the same. Your teacher’s chart is showing these different views, which we call moon phases.

You can watch it change yourself! Try looking up at the sky around the same time each evening for a few weeks. You’ll see it slowly grow bigger, then smaller, and then back to a circle again. It’s a steady cycle that takes about a month to complete. Let me know if you’d like to know what each shape is called!

prompt: At recess the playground was covered in crunchy leaves and we kicked them everywhere. My friend said the trees are 'going to sleep.' Why do leaves fall in autumn?

response.1:
Your friend has a really nice way of describing it! Trees do get ready for a long rest, kind of like how we sleep to recharge.

In autumn, the days get shorter and the weather starts to cool down. Trees notice this change and begin to prepare for the colder months. They slowly stop using sunlight to make food in their leaves and pull back the water and nutrients they need to stay strong. As the leaves lose their green color and turn yellow, orange, or brown, they become dry and light. Then, a gentle breeze or even a little shake is enough to make them let go.

This helps the tree save energy and protect itself during winter. When spring arrives and the sun gets warmer again, the tree will “wake up” and grow fresh new leaves. It’s a natural cycle that keeps trees healthy year after year. Next time you’re outside, you can watch how the leaves change color before they fall—it’s a quiet way nature gets ready for the seasons!

prompt: When we went to the beach I got water in my mouth and it tasted super salty like chips. Nobody put salt in it, so why is the ocean salty?

response.1:
That’s a really good question! The ocean tastes salty because salt has been slowly collecting in it for millions of years. Even though nobody pours salt into it, nature does it in a simple way.

Rain falls on rocks and soil on land and picks up tiny bits of minerals, including salt. Rivers carry that salty water all the way to the ocean. When the sun warms the ocean, the water turns into vapor and floats up into the sky to make clouds again. But the salt is too heavy to float away, so it stays behind in the water. 

It’s a bit like when you boil a pot of water with a little salt in it. The water turns to steam and floats away, but the salt stays in the pot. The ocean has been doing this for millions of years, so all that salt has built up and makes the water taste salty!

Does that help explain it? Let me know if you’re curious about anything else about the ocean or weather!

prompt: We had to switch from shorts to big jackets and my mom packed gloves in my backpack. Why does the weather change like that? Why do we have seasons?

response.1:
That’s a wonderful question! The reason the weather changes and we have seasons is because of how the Earth moves around the Sun.

The Earth travels in a big circle around the Sun, but it doesn’t stand up straight. It leans a little to one side, like a spinning top that’s slightly tilted. Because of this tilt, different parts of the Earth get more or less sunlight at different times of the year.

When your part of the world leans toward the Sun, the sunlight hits us more directly and feels warm—that’s summer, when you can wear shorts. When it leans away, the sunlight is weaker and spread out, so it feels cooler—that’s winter, when you need a jacket and gloves. Spring and autumn are the times in between when the tilt is more balanced.

A lot of people think seasons happen because the Earth gets closer or farther from the Sun, but that’s not true. It’s really just that tilt changing how much sun we get. This yearly cycle is what helps crops grow, animals prepare for colder months, and us change our clothes!

If you’d like, you could ask your mom, a teacher, or an older cousin to sketch a quick picture of the Earth and Sun with you. It’s a fun way to see how the tilt works. Let me know if you’re curious about anything else about weather or the Earth!

prompt: My dad told me not to stare at the sun because it could hurt my eyes. If it's so far away, why is the sun so bright?

response.1:
Your dad is right to tell you not to stare at the sun. Even though the sun is very far away, it is also incredibly huge and powerful. Think of it like a bright streetlight or a campfire: even from a distance, the light is still strong because the source itself is so big and energetic. The sun is like the biggest light in the sky. Its light travels all the way to Earth to warm us, help plants grow, and light up our days.

But because it is so powerful, looking straight at it can hurt the delicate parts of your eyes, just like how a very bright camera flash makes you want to look away. That’s why it’s always best to enjoy the sun safely, like watching it set when it’s lower and softer, or looking at it through clouds. If you’re curious about how the sun works, you could ask your dad, a teacher, or an older cousin to help you find a fun book or video about space!

prompt: After it rained, I saw a rainbow and ran to tell my teacher before it disappeared. Where did it come from? Why do rainbows appear?

response.1:
That’s a wonderful thing to notice! Rainbows are one of nature’s most beautiful sights.

A rainbow comes from sunlight meeting raindrops in the air. Even though sunlight looks white to us, it’s actually made of all the colors mixed together. When sunlight passes through a raindrop, the drop acts like a tiny glass prism. It bends the light and splits it into the separate colors we can see: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet.

You can only see a rainbow when the sun is shining from behind you and the rain is in front of you. Once the rain stops or the clouds move and block the sun, the light no longer passes through the drops the same way, and the rainbow fades away. 

It’s a bit like how a clear glass of water or a shiny stone can sometimes show little flashes of color when the sun hits it just right. Next time you see one, you’ll know it’s sunlight and raindrops working together to paint the sky!

prompt: At recess I lay on the grass and watched clouds move like cotton balls. They look heavy. Why don’t they fall down? Why do clouds float?

response.1:
That’s a wonderful thing to notice! Clouds do look heavy, but there’s a simple reason they stay up in the sky.

Clouds are made of millions of tiny water droplets or ice crystals. Even though a whole cloud can weigh a lot, each tiny drop is so small and light that it doesn’t fall right away. 

Think of how dust floats in a sunbeam, or how a feather stays in the air when you blow on it. Warm air from the ground rises up and pushes those tiny drops upward. This rising air holds the cloud up, and the wind carries it across the sky, which is why clouds seem to move.

Clouds do fall down, but only when the tiny drops bump into each other and grow bigger and heavier. When they get too heavy for the rising air to hold, they fall as rain or snow!

Next time you’re at recess, you can watch for clouds that look dark and puffy—those are usually the ones getting ready to rain. Keep enjoying your sky watching!

prompt: We had indoor recess because it was pouring outside and I was mad. Who turns the rain on? Why does it rain?

response.1:
It’s completely okay to feel frustrated when you have to stay inside during recess. I know it’s fun to run and play outside!

To answer your question: nobody actually turns the rain on like a tap. Rain happens naturally. Here’s how it works:

The sun warms up water from rivers, lakes, and the sea. That warm water turns into an invisible gas that floats up into the sky. As it goes higher, the air gets cooler, and the gas turns back into tiny water droplets. These droplets stick together to form clouds. When the clouds get too heavy to hold all that water, the drops fall back down to Earth as rain.

Think of it like a giant, natural sponge. The sky soaks up water, gets full, and then gently squeezes it back down. After the rain stops, the water soaks into the ground, fills up rivers, and the whole cycle starts again.

Even though you can’t play outside right now, you could try watching the rain from a window, drawing what you see, or asking your teacher if you can go out for a few minutes once the ground dries a bit. Would you like to know how rainbows form after it rains?

prompt: I wanted to keep playing my game but my mom said bedtime is important. If I’m not tired yet, why do we even need to sleep?

response.1:
It’s completely normal to want to keep playing, especially when you’re having fun! Even if you don’t feel sleepy yet, your body and brain still need that rest time. Think of sleep like saving your progress in a game or charging a device. While you’re asleep, your body is quietly growing, repairing your muscles, and sorting out everything you learned and did during the day.

If you skip that rest, you might find it harder to focus in school, feel grumpy, or not play as well the next day. Your mom knows that your body needs that quiet time to get ready for tomorrow, even when you don’t feel tired yet.

If you’re having trouble winding down, you could try reading a book, listening to calm music, or chatting with your mom or another family member about your day before lights out. I hope you have a fun and energetic day tomorrow!

prompt: During reading time I yawned and then my friend yawned too. It felt like it spread. Why do we yawn?

response.1:
That’s a really good observation! Yawning can definitely “spread,” and scientists have a few helpful ideas about why it happens.

We yawn for a few main reasons. First, it helps cool down our brains. Just like a fan cools down a room, a big yawn brings in cool air and helps keep our brain at the right temperature. Second, it helps us wake up or get ready for rest. Yawning stretches our lungs and jaw, which can help us feel more alert when we’re sleepy, or help our body relax when it’s time to wind down. It also helps our body take a good, deep breath.

As for why your friend yawned right after you, that’s called “contagious yawning.” Our brains are naturally tuned to notice what the people around us are doing. When you see someone yawn, your brain kind of copies it. It’s actually a sign that you’re paying attention to each other and feel connected! It happens a lot with friends, family, and even pets.

Scientists are still learning all the details, but it’s completely normal. So next time you yawn during reading time, you can just smile—it’s just your body doing its job, and your friend’s brain was simply being in sync with yours!

prompt: My teacher said blinking keeps our eyes healthy but I don’t even notice doing it. Why do we blink?

response.1:
Blinking is something your body does automatically to take care of your eyes. Even though you don’t notice it, your eyes blink about 15 to 20 times every minute! Here’s why it’s so important:

• It spreads a thin layer of tears across your eyes to keep them moist and comfortable.
• It gently washes away tiny bits of dust, pollen, or dirt that might try to get in.
• It gives your eyes a quick little rest, kind of like how you close your eyes when you’re tired or daydreaming.

Your brain controls blinking without you having to think about it, just like breathing or your heart beating. So whether you’re reading a book, watching a show, or playing outside, your eyes are getting the care they need. If you’d like, you can try blinking slowly on purpose a few times and notice how clean and refreshed your eyes feel afterward!

prompt: Before lunch my stomach makes growling noises and my friends laugh. Why do we get hungry like that?

response.1:
Your stomach growls because it’s getting ready for food! When your stomach is empty, it starts to gently squeeze. These squeezes move the air and a little bit of liquid around inside, which makes that rumbling or growling sound. It’s actually your body’s natural way of saying, “It’s time to eat!” Everyone’s stomach does this, even grown-ups, so it’s completely normal.

If your friends laugh, you can just smile and tell them it means your tummy is ready for lunch. If you want to quiet it down a bit, you could ask a parent, aunt, or other trusted adult if you can keep a small snack, like a biscuit or a piece of fruit, in your school bag to eat before lunchtime. Your body is just doing exactly what it’s supposed to do!

prompt: After running laps in gym my legs felt like jelly. Why do we feel tired after running?

response.1:
When you run, your leg muscles work like little engines that use up the energy from your food. They also need extra oxygen, so your heart and lungs work harder to send it to your legs. After running for a while, your muscles get temporarily tired and send a “rest now” signal to your brain. That’s what makes them feel wobbly or like jelly.

This is completely normal and actually a good sign—it means your muscles are learning to get stronger. To help them recover, drink some water, rest for a few minutes, and gently stretch your legs. Next time you have gym class, try warming up with a light walk first and take short breaks if you need them. Your body will thank you!

prompt: In gym class we ran around cones and I could feel my heart thumping in my chest. Why does our heart beat faster when we run?

response.1:
That’s a great question! Your heart beats faster when you run because your muscles need more energy and oxygen to keep moving.

Think of your heart like a pump. When you’re sitting or walking slowly, it pumps blood at a calm, steady pace. But when you run around those cones, your leg muscles work much harder. They need extra oxygen and nutrients from your blood to keep going. So, your brain sends a quick message to your heart: “Pump faster!” This sends more blood to your muscles so you can keep running.

It’s a lot like a delivery person speeding up when there are many packages to drop off. Your heart is just making sure your muscles get what they need! Once you stop running and rest, your muscles don’t need as much extra blood, so your heart slowly goes back to its normal, calm rhythm.

It’s completely normal to feel that thumping—it just means your body is working exactly how it should! Next time you run, you can even try feeling your pulse right after you stop, then again after a minute of resting, to watch it slow down. Keep enjoying gym class!

prompt: I told my mom about a dream where I was flying over school. My brain made it up while I was asleep. Why do we dream?

response.1:
That sounds like a fun dream! Flying over your school must have felt exciting. You’re right that your brain creates dreams while you sleep.

Scientists aren’t completely sure why we dream, but they have some good ideas. When you sleep, your brain doesn’t just turn off. It stays busy sorting through everything you saw, heard, and felt during the day. Think of it like your brain tidying up a messy room—putting important memories in the right places and letting go of things you don’t need. Sometimes, while it’s doing this work, it mixes ideas together in surprising ways, like making you fly!

Dreams also help your brain practice handling feelings. If you were excited about school, thinking about a game, or even a little worried about something, your brain might turn those feelings into a dream story.

So, dreaming is mostly your brain’s way of resting, learning, and keeping your mind healthy. Everyone dreams, even if they don’t always remember them. If you ever have a dream that feels really strange or makes you feel upset, it’s always okay to talk about it with your mom, dad, or another grown-up you trust, like an aunt, uncle, or grandparent. They can help you understand it too.

prompt: In class someone sneezed super loud and scared everyone. Why does that happen? Why do we sneeze?

response.1:
Sneezing is your body’s quick way of cleaning your nose. When tiny things like dust, pollen, pet hair, or a cold germ float into your nose, your body wants to push them out. It sends a fast signal to your brain, and your brain tells your chest and nose muscles to squeeze together suddenly. That pushes a burst of air out of your nose and mouth, which makes the "achoo!" sound.

A sneeze can sound extra loud or scary because the air comes out very fast, and it happens without warning. It’s a lot like a balloon popping or a door slamming suddenly—our ears and brains are wired to notice loud, unexpected sounds, so it’s normal that it startled your classmates. It doesn’t mean anything is wrong; it just means that person’s body was doing its job to keep them healthy.

If you ever feel a sneeze coming, it’s a good habit to cover your mouth with a tissue or the inside of your elbow, and you can quietly say "excuse me" so it doesn’t surprise people. Next time you hear a loud sneeze, you can smile and say "Bless you" or "Khuda pakiz" to be kind. Let me know if you’d like to know more about how your body protects you!

prompt: At lunch I got hiccups and my friend tried to scare me to fix it. Why do we hiccup anyway?

response.1:
Hiccups happen when a muscle under your lungs called the diaphragm gets a little twitchy. This muscle helps you breathe, and when it suddenly tightens, it makes that quick “hic!” sound. You might get hiccups if you eat or drink too fast, swallow a lot of air, have a very cold or fizzy drink, or even if you’re laughing or excited.

Your friend probably tried to scare you because some people think a quick surprise can help “reset” that muscle and stop the hiccups. It’s a common trick, but it doesn’t always work. Most of the time, hiccups go away on their own in a few minutes. If they don’t stop, trying to sip some warm water slowly or taking a few calm, deep breaths can help.

If your hiccups last for a very long time or happen to you a lot, it’s a good idea to let a parent, aunt, uncle, or teacher know so they can check on you. Otherwise, just relax—they’re usually nothing to worry about!

prompt: When it’s cold waiting for the bus, I get tiny bumps on my arms. Why do we get goosebumps?

response.1:
That’s a great question! Those tiny bumps are called goosebumps, and they happen because of a little trick your body tries to do when it’s cold.

Under your skin, there are tiny muscles attached to where each hair grows. When you feel cold, those muscles quickly pull up, making your hairs stand straight and creating little bumps on your skin. 

A long time ago, our human ancestors had much thicker body hair, just like many animals do today. When animals get cold, their fur stands up to trap a layer of warm air close to their skin, like a built-in blanket. Humans don’t have thick body hair anymore, so goosebumps don’t keep us very warm, but our bodies still do it out of habit!

You might also get them when you’re excited, scared, or listening to a favorite song. It’s completely normal and just means your body is reacting to what you’re feeling. Next time you’re waiting for the bus, try wrapping your arms around yourself or putting on a warm jacket—that will keep you cozy much better than goosebumps can!

prompt: Our dog’s tail goes crazy when my dad gets home. Is he talking with it? Why do dogs wag their tails?

response.1:
Dogs don’t use their tails to talk with words, but they do use them to show how they feel. Think of a dog’s tail like a feeling flag! When your dad walks through the door, your dog is probably feeling very excited and glad to see him. Wagging is one of the main ways dogs say, “I’m so happy you’re home!”

Dogs “talk” with their whole body. They use their ears, their barks, how they stand, and yes, their tails. A big, loose wag usually means excitement or friendliness. Sometimes dogs wag when they’re a little unsure or nervous, too, but when it happens right when someone they love comes home, it’s almost always a happy greeting.

It’s kind of like how you might smile really big, jump up, or run to hug someone when they arrive. Your dog is just showing love in his own special way. If you watch closely, you’ll notice his ears and whole body move with the wag—that’s his way of saying hello!

prompt: When I pet my cat she makes a tiny motor sound. Why do cats purr?

response.1:
Cats purr for a few different reasons, and it’s a really special sound! When you pet your cat and she makes that tiny motor noise, she is mostly telling you that she feels happy, safe, and comfortable with you. It’s her way of saying, “I like this!”

Cats also purr when they are feeling a little hurt, nervous, or tired. Scientists believe the gentle vibrations from purring can actually help them feel calm and even help their bodies heal, kind of like how a warm blanket or a quiet room helps you relax.

So when your cat purrs while you’re petting her, it’s a good sign that she trusts you and is enjoying your company. You can keep giving her gentle pets and talking to her softly. If she ever stops purring or walks away, that just means she’s had enough pets for now, and it’s okay to give her some space.

prompt: We watched birds outside the classroom window and they just flew away. Why can birds fly but we can’t?

response.1:
That’s a wonderful question! Birds and humans are just built for different things. Birds have special bodies that make flying easy for them. Their bones are light and have tiny air pockets inside, which keeps them strong but not heavy. They also have very strong chest muscles to flap their wings, and their feathers are shaped to catch the air and lift them up, kind of like how a kite catches the wind.

Our bodies are built differently. We have heavier bones and strong legs that are perfect for walking, running, jumping, and climbing. We don’t have wings or feathers, so we can’t fly. But that’s okay! Humans are really good at using our hands and brains to build things that fly, like airplanes, kites, and paper planes.

It’s like how a bicycle is made for riding and a car is made for driving—birds and people are just designed for different jobs! If you’d like to see how flight works, you could try folding a paper airplane or making a simple kite and watch how the air lifts it up.

prompt: On our aquarium trip the fish never came out of the water. Why do fish live in water all the time?

response.1:
That’s a great observation! Fish live in water all the time because their bodies are specially built for it. Here’s why:

- **They breathe through gills:** Fish have gills on the sides of their heads that pull oxygen out of water. If a fish comes out of the water, its gills stick together and it can’t get the air it needs. It’s a bit like how you would struggle to breathe if your nose and mouth were covered.
- **Water holds them up:** Fish don’t have strong legs or heavy bones like we do. Water is thick and helps support their bodies so they can swim without getting tired. On land, they would feel too heavy and couldn’t move properly.
- **They need to stay wet:** A fish’s skin and scales are made to keep moisture in and protect them. Out of water, they would quickly dry out and get sick.

That’s why you’ll always see them swimming in tanks, rivers, or oceans! Next time you visit an aquarium, you can watch how their gills gently move in and out—that’s them breathing underwater. Let me know if you want to learn about how different fish are built for different kinds of water!

prompt: Our science book said bees make honey for themselves. Why do bees make honey?

response.1: Bees make honey to store food for later, just like how you might keep extra snacks in your kitchen for a day when you can’t go out. During warm months, bees visit flowers to collect a sweet liquid called nectar. They bring it back to their hive and work together to turn it into thick, sweet honey. This honey becomes their main food, especially in winter or during dry seasons when flowers aren’t blooming. So your science book is right—bees make honey to feed themselves and their whole hive when fresh nectar isn’t available. It’s their way of making sure no one goes hungry!

prompt: My teacher said bears sleep all winter. Why do some animals hibernate?

response.1:
That’s a wonderful question! Hibernation is a special kind of deep rest that some animals use to survive the winter.

During winter, the weather gets very cold and food like plants, insects, and berries becomes very hard to find. Instead of using up all their energy searching for food, hibernating animals find a safe, cozy place to rest and let their bodies slow down. Their heartbeat and breathing become very slow, and their body temperature drops. They live off the extra fat they stored up before winter, kind of like how you might pack extra snacks for a long car ride.

You’re right that bears hibernate, but they don’t sleep the exact same way we do. They might wake up a little sometimes, but they stay in their dens to keep warm and save energy. Other animals that hibernate include groundhogs, bats, hedgehogs, and some frogs. In the northern mountains of Pakistan, animals like marmots also go into a long winter rest to survive the heavy snow.

When spring arrives, the weather warms up, food becomes available again, and the animals wake up hungry and ready to explore! If you’d like to learn more, you could ask your teacher about other animals that prepare for winter, or look for a children’s book with pictures of hibernating animals. Let me know if you have more questions!

prompt: I saw a giraffe video and its neck was super long. Why do giraffes have long necks?

response.1:
Giraffes have long necks for two main reasons: to reach food and to stay safe. In the wild, they eat leaves from tall trees that other animals can’t reach. This gives them plenty of food without having to compete. Their long necks also act like a lookout tower, helping them see over tall grass to spot danger, like lions, from far away.

Scientists believe giraffes’ necks grew longer over many, many generations. Long ago, giraffes with slightly longer necks could find more food and stay safer, so they lived longer and had more babies. Those babies inherited the longer necks, and over time, that became the normal way giraffes look today.

It’s a great example of how animals slowly change to fit where they live! Let me know if you want to learn about other amazing animals.

prompt: Penguins have wings but they just waddle. Why don’t penguins fly?

response.1:
Penguins actually *do* use their wings, but not for flying in the air! Their wings are shaped like flippers, which makes them amazing swimmers. Underwater, they flap their wings to push through the water, kind of like flying through the sea.

The reason they don’t fly in the sky is that their bodies are built for life in cold water. Their bones are heavy and solid (instead of light and hollow like flying birds), and their feathers are thick and waterproof to keep them warm. All of that makes them too heavy to lift off the ground. Their legs are also short and set far back on their bodies, which is perfect for swimming but makes them waddle on land.

So, penguins traded flying in the air for being champion swimmers! If you ever watch a video of a penguin underwater, you’ll see how gracefully they move. Let me know if you want to learn about other animals that swim instead of fly!

prompt: We saw a frog near the sidewalk and it bounced away fast. Why do frogs jump instead of walk?

response.1:
Frogs jump because their bodies are built like little springs! They have very long, strong back legs and a flexible spine that lets them push off the ground with a lot of power. Jumping is also a smart way for them to stay safe. If a bird, snake, or other animal comes too close, a quick jump helps them get away fast. It also helps them catch bugs for food.

Some frogs can actually walk or hop slowly when they don’t need to rush, but jumping is just their fastest and most natural way to move. Next time you see one, you might notice how their back legs are much bigger than their front legs—that’s their jumping secret!

prompt: In the school garden I saw butterflies with bright colors. Why do butterflies have colorful wings?

response.1:
Butterflies have colorful wings for a few clever reasons:

• **To find a partner:** Bright colors help butterflies spot each other in the garden so they can find a mate and have babies.
• **To stay safe:** Some bright colors act like a warning sign. They tell birds or other animals, “I taste bad or I’m not safe to eat!” Other patterns, like dark spots, can look like big eyes to surprise or scare them away.
• **To hide:** Some butterflies have colors that match leaves, tree bark, or flowers. This helps them blend in and rest safely.
• **To stay warm:** Darker colors soak up the sun’s heat. This warms up their wings so they can fly more easily.

The colors actually come from thousands of tiny, flat scales on their wings, kind of like the shingles on a roof. When sunlight hits them, they reflect different colors. 

It’s wonderful that you noticed them in your school garden! Next time you see one, you can watch how it opens and closes its wings to catch the sun or hide among the plants. Let me know if you want to learn about a specific butterfly you saw!

prompt: My teacher gave us math homework again and I groaned. Why do we have homework?

response.1:
It’s completely normal to sigh when you hear about homework! Homework is basically practice for your brain. Think of it like learning a new game, rehearsing a poem, or practicing a sport—you get better and more confident the more you try it. In math, homework helps you remember the steps you learned in class and gives you a chance to solve problems on your own. It also helps your teacher see what you’ve mastered and where you might need a little extra help.

If math homework ever feels too heavy, try these simple steps:
- Break it into small pieces and tackle one or two problems at a time.
- Take a short break to stretch or drink some water if you feel stuck.
- Ask a parent, older sibling, cousin, or another trusted relative to sit with you for a bit. You don’t have to get every answer right the first time—making mistakes is just part of learning.

Keep going, and if something feels really confusing, it’s always okay to ask your teacher or a trusted adult for help. You’re doing great just by keeping at it!

prompt: We do so many math problems every day. Why do we learn math?

response.1:
It’s completely normal to feel tired of all those worksheets! Math might seem like just numbers on a page, but it’s actually a tool we use every single day, even when we don’t notice. Here’s why we learn it:

• **Shopping and money:** When you go to the bazaar or help buy groceries, math helps you count change, compare prices, and make sure you’re getting a fair deal.
• **Cooking and baking:** Making food is like a math experiment. You need to measure cups, spoons, and time so your roti, chai, or cake turns out right.
• **Time and planning:** Math helps you figure out how long it takes to get to school, when to start your homework, or how much time you have before a cricket match or family visit.
• **Problem-solving:** Math trains your brain to think step-by-step. This helps you solve puzzles, fix things, or figure out fair ways to share snacks with friends.
• **Future dreams:** Whether you want to be a doctor, engineer, artist, shopkeeper, or athlete, math is used in almost every job and hobby. It helps you understand patterns, build things, and even keep score in games.

Practicing math problems is a lot like training for a sport. At first it feels hard, but the more you practice, the stronger and faster your brain gets. If you ever feel stuck, it’s okay to ask your teacher, a cousin, or a trusted adult like your mama, phupho, or grandparents to help you work through it. Keep going—you’re building skills that will help you navigate the world every day!

prompt: My mom makes me read before bed even when I want to watch cartoons. Why do we need to read books?

response.1:
It’s completely normal to want to watch cartoons, especially when you’re tired or just want to relax. Your mom likely has you read before bed because books are really good for your growing brain and your daily life.

Reading helps you learn new words, understand stories better, and do well in school. It also gives your imagination a chance to build pictures in your mind, which is a fun kind of mental exercise. Many of the best stories, adventures, and lessons are found in books, and the more you read, the easier it becomes to understand the world around you.

There’s also a good reason your mom picks bedtime for it. Cartoons are bright, loud, and fast, which can sometimes make it harder for your body to settle down. A quiet book helps your eyes and brain wind down, making it easier to fall asleep and wake up feeling rested.

If reading feels like a chore, you could try picking books that match things you already enjoy—like adventure stories, funny tales, or books with lots of pictures. You might also ask your mom if you could read for a little while first, and then watch one short cartoon as a treat. Most parents are happy to find a balance that works for both of you.

Keep asking questions like this—it shows you’re thinking carefully about how things work, and that’s a wonderful habit to have.

prompt: Everyone gets nervous before a test in class. Why do teachers give tests?

response.1:
It’s very normal to feel nervous before a test. Teachers give tests for a few helpful reasons:

• To see what you’ve learned so far. This helps them know if you’re ready for new lessons or if you might need a little extra practice.
• To help your brain remember better. When you study and answer questions, you’re practicing how to pull information out, which makes it stick.
• To share a clear update with you and your family about how you’re doing in class.

Tests aren’t meant to trick you or make you feel bad. Think of them like a checkpoint on a long walk—they just show where you are and what you might want to focus on next. If you’re feeling nervous, try getting a good night’s sleep, eating a light snack, and taking a few slow breaths before the test. You can also talk to your teacher, a parent, or a trusted family member like an aunt, uncle, or older cousin about how you’re feeling. They can help you feel more prepared and calm.

prompt: Sometimes I want to stay home and play games instead of going to school. Why do we have to go every day?

response.1:
It’s completely normal to feel that way! Games are fun, and staying home can feel cozy and relaxing. Many kids feel the same way sometimes.

We go to school every day because it’s where we learn the skills we’ll need to grow up and do the things we love. School teaches you how to read, solve problems, work with others, and discover new interests. Those skills help you later in life—whether you want to design video games, build things, help your family, or explore the world. Families and communities often see school as an important step toward building a good future and being able to take care of yourself and others when you’re older.

That doesn’t mean you can’t enjoy games! A good balance is to finish your schoolwork and responsibilities first, then set aside a special time for play. You could even ask a parent, aunt, uncle, or older cousin to help you make a simple daily schedule that includes time for homework, games, and rest.

If you’re feeling really tired or stressed about school, it’s okay to talk to a trusted adult at home. They can help you figure out what’s making school feel heavy and find ways to make it easier. You’ve got this!

prompt: My friend at recess said water isn’t really wet and we argued about it. So why is water wet?

response.1:
That’s a really fun question, and it’s one that even scientists sometimes talk about! The answer actually depends on how you define the word “wet.”

If you think “wet” means a liquid that is sticking to a solid, then water itself isn’t wet. Water is the liquid that makes other things wet. For example, when you wash your hands, the water makes your skin wet, but the water is just being water.

But if you think “wet” means something that feels cool, slippery, and can soak into things, then yes, water is wet! Water naturally sticks to itself and to other surfaces, which is what gives that wet feeling.

So both you and your friend have good points! You could tell them that you’re both right, depending on how you look at it. Next time you’re at recess, you could try a quick test: dip a dry cloth or paper towel into a cup of water. The cloth gets wet, but the water stays water. What do you think makes more sense to you?

prompt: I put an ice cube in my drink and it disappeared. Why does ice melt?

response.1:
Ice melts because it is picking up warmth from its surroundings. Ice is just water that has frozen into a solid shape. When you drop an ice cube into a drink, the drink is warmer than the ice. That warmth moves into the ice, giving it enough energy to change back into liquid water. So the ice doesn’t really disappear—it just turns into water and mixes right into your drink!

You can see the same thing happen when snow turns into puddles on a sunny day, or when you leave a frozen treat out on the counter and it slowly turns into a puddle.

If you ever want to keep ice from melting quickly, you can put it in a cooler or wrap it in a cloth to keep the warmth out. Let me know if you’d like to know more about how water changes shape!

prompt: At a campfire my dad said not to touch the flames. Why is fire so hot?

response.1:
Fire is hot because it’s releasing energy. When something like wood or paper burns, the tiny pieces that make it up start moving very, very fast. That fast movement creates both light and heat.

Your skin isn’t built to handle that kind of energy, so if you touch a flame, it can hurt you almost instantly. That’s why your dad told you to keep your hands away—it’s a simple, caring rule to keep you safe while you enjoy the campfire.

If you ever want to see how movement can make heat, try rubbing your palms together quickly. You’ll feel a little warmth, but fire is thousands of times stronger, so it’s always best to watch it from a safe distance. Let me know if you’re curious about anything else about fire or campfires!

prompt: In science class the magnet stuck to my locker but not my notebook. Why do magnets stick to some things?

response.1:
Magnets stick to certain kinds of metals, like the steel or iron used to make your locker. They don’t stick to materials like paper, wood, or plastic, which is why it didn’t stick to your notebook.

Inside metals like iron and steel, there are tiny parts that act like little magnets. When a real magnet comes close, those tiny parts line up and pull toward it. In things like paper or plastic, those parts don’t line up, so there’s no pull at all.

You can try a quick test: see if your magnet sticks to a metal spoon, a paperclip, a coin, or a pencil case. You’ll notice it only sticks to certain metals, not to everything.

If you want to learn more, ask your science teacher or a trusted grown-up. They can show you fun, safe ways to keep exploring how magnets work!

prompt: When I walk under the streetlight at night, a dark shape follows me. Why do shadows appear?

response.1:
That dark shape is just your shadow, and it’s completely normal to notice it at night! Shadows happen when something blocks light. Light travels in straight lines, and when you stand between a light source (like a streetlight or the sun) and the ground, your body stops the light from reaching that spot. The dark area behind you is simply the place where the light can’t get through.

It looks like it’s following you because as you move, you keep blocking the light, so the dark shape moves with you. It’s not a real object or a spirit—it’s just a natural trick of light and dark. You can easily see how it works at home: turn on a lamp and hold your hand up. You’ll see a dark shape on the wall that moves exactly when you move your hand.

Shadows can look a little spooky in the dark, but they’re completely harmless. If you ever feel uneasy walking at night, it’s always a good idea to walk with a parent, older sibling, or another trusted family member. Otherwise, you can just enjoy watching how your shadow changes size and shape depending on where the light is! Let me know if you’d like to know more about how light works.

prompt: At my birthday party the balloons went up to the ceiling and stayed there. Why do balloons float?

response.1:
Balloons float because they are filled with a gas that is lighter than the air around us. Most party balloons are filled with helium. Even though we can’t see it, the air in our room actually has weight. When a balloon is filled with helium, it becomes lighter than the air it pushes out of the way.

Think of it like a cork in a glass of water. The cork is lighter than water, so it floats to the top. In the same way, the helium balloon is lighter than the air in your room, so it floats all the way up to the ceiling. Once it hits the ceiling, it stays there because there’s nowhere lighter for it to go!

If you blow up a balloon with just your breath, it won’t float. That’s because the air from your lungs is heavier than helium, so it just falls down.

It’s a fun little science trick that makes birthday parties feel magical! Next time you see a balloon, you can imagine it gently pushing the heavier air out of its way as it floats up.

prompt: My friends started giggling in class and then I couldn’t stop laughing either. Why do we laugh?

response.1:
Laughing is a natural way our bodies and brains show that we feel happy, surprised, or even a little silly. When your friends started giggling, your brain probably noticed their happy sounds and faces, and it wanted to join in! This is very common and is sometimes called "social laughter." Humans are wired to connect with each other, so when we hear others laughing, our own brains often follow along. It’s like when a funny joke makes the whole room laugh together.

Laughing also gives your body a little boost of feel-good energy, which is why it can be hard to stop once it starts. It’s completely normal to catch yourself laughing just because your friends are laughing. If it happens during a quiet part of class, you can take a slow breath, sip some water, or gently remind yourself to pause until break time. Otherwise, just enjoy the moment—laughing with friends is a healthy and happy thing!

prompt: I dropped my pencil in class and it fell to the floor. Why do things fall down instead of up?

response.1:
That’s a wonderful question! Things fall down because of an invisible force called **gravity**. Gravity is Earth’s way of gently pulling everything toward its center. It’s what keeps your feet on the ground, holds your books on your desk, and makes your pencil drop to the floor when it slips from your hand.

You can think of it like a steady, invisible tug that keeps all objects close to the ground. Without gravity, you, your pencil, and even the air would float away into space! That’s why when you jump, you always come back down, and why balls roll toward the floor instead of floating up to the ceiling.

Gravity is one of the reasons our world stays steady and safe. If you ever want to know more about how it works or how it affects things like the Moon or oceans, just ask!

prompt: My dad said the car won’t move unless we put gas in it. Why do cars need fuel?

response.1:
Cars need fuel for the same reason you need food: to get energy! 

Inside a car’s engine, the fuel mixes with air and burns in a very controlled way. This burning creates tiny, powerful pushes that the engine catches and turns into spinning motion for the wheels. Without fuel, the engine has no energy to make those pushes, so the car stays still.

Think of it like riding a bicycle. You can’t pedal forever without getting tired because your body uses up energy. A car’s engine uses fuel as its “food” to keep going. When the tank is empty, it’s like the car is hungry and needs to be refilled before it can go on another trip.

If you’re curious, I can also explain how the fuel travels from the tank to the engine, or how electric cars work instead!

prompt: The dentist said I have to brush or I’ll get cavities. Why do we brush our teeth?

response.1:
We brush our teeth to keep them strong and healthy. When we eat or drink, tiny bits of food get stuck between our teeth. If we don’t clean them out, tiny germs start to grow. These germs love sugar, especially from treats like jalebi, gulab jamun, or even juice. When the germs eat the sugar, they make a sour acid that slowly weakens your teeth and creates tiny holes called cavities.

Brushing with toothpaste sweeps away the food bits and washes the germs down the drain. It also leaves a protective layer on your teeth so they stay strong. If you brush twice a day, you’ll keep your smile bright and avoid those ouchy cavities. Next time you enjoy a sweet snack, just remember to brush afterward so your teeth stay happy!

prompt: We have a plant by the classroom window and the teacher said it needs sun to grow. Why do plants need sunlight?

response.1:
Plants need sunlight because it gives them the energy to make their own food. Just like you eat meals to grow strong and have energy to play, plants need food too—but they make it right inside their leaves!

When sunlight touches a plant’s leaves, the plant uses that light like a power source. It mixes water from the soil with air from around it to create a natural sugar. This sugar is the plant’s food. It helps the plant grow taller, make new leaves, and stay healthy.

Without enough sunlight, a plant can’t make enough food. That’s why plants kept in dark places often look pale, droopy, or stop growing. Your classroom plant is by the window so it can get the “power” it needs to thrive.

You can even watch it over the next few weeks. If it gets plenty of sun, you’ll likely see it grow new leaves or look greener and stronger!

prompt: My clock makes a tick-tock sound at night and I can hear it when I’m trying to sleep. Why do clocks tick?

response.1:
Clocks tick because of the tiny moving parts inside them that work together to count time. Most ticking clocks have little gears and a spring or a pendulum that slowly release energy. As the gears turn, they move in small, steady steps. Each step makes a little click, and the back-and-forth movement creates the familiar "tick-tock" sound. It’s kind of like how your footsteps make a steady rhythm when you walk, or how a heartbeat goes thump-thump. The clock is just keeping a steady beat so it can tell you the right time.

If the sound makes it hard to fall asleep, you could try placing a soft cloth or a small pillow over the clock, moving it a little farther from your bed, or asking a parent, aunt, or another trusted adult to help you find a quieter one. I hope you get some good rest!

prompt: My mom says I can’t just run outside in my pajamas. Why do we wear clothes?

response.1:
We wear clothes for a few important reasons. First, they protect your skin from the hot sun, wind, dust, scratches, and bugs, and they help keep you warm or cool depending on the weather. Second, in our culture, wearing proper clothes outside shows respect for yourself and for the people you meet. It’s a way of following the good manners and values your family teaches you. Third, different clothes are meant for different places. Pajamas are made for sleeping and staying comfortably inside your home, while outside clothes are made for being out in the world where there’s more dust, sun, and people around. 

Your mom’s rule isn’t just about being strict—she wants you to be comfortable, protected, and ready to show respect when you’re outside. If you ever aren’t sure what to wear, you can always ask her or another trusted adult like an aunt, uncle, or older cousin to help you pick something that’s both comfortable and appropriate. Let me know if you’d like tips on picking good outside clothes!

prompt: At my friend’s birthday party we sang and ate cake and gave presents. Why do we celebrate birthdays every year?

response.1:
We celebrate birthdays every year to mark the time that has passed since the day someone was born. A year is about 365 days, which is how long it takes for the Earth to travel all the way around the Sun. When that time comes around again, it means the person has lived one more full year.

Birthdays are a happy way to show love and appreciation. They give families and friends a special reason to gather, share food, give small gifts, and make a wish for the year ahead. Many people also say a short dua for good health and happiness. 

Think of a birthday like a milestone on a path. It helps us notice how much someone has grown, learned new things, and changed. It’s also a lovely excuse to spend time together and make good memories.

If you’re curious about how your own family likes to celebrate, you could ask your parents, a favorite aunt or uncle, or even your grandparents!

prompt: In my class some kids speak another language at home and their parents sound different on the phone. Why do people have different languages?

response.1:
That’s a really thoughtful question! People speak different languages because they grow up in different places and families. Just like how you learn the words, songs, and ways of talking that your family uses at home, other kids learn the language their parents and community use every day.

When you hear parents sound different on the phone, it’s usually because they’re speaking the language they grew up with, or they’re using the natural rhythm and sounds from their hometown. Our brains learn to make those sounds from the very first time we start talking, so everyone’s voice carries a little bit of where they come from.

In Pakistan, it’s very common for families to speak different languages at home—like Punjabi, Sindhi, Pashto, Balochi, or Urdu—while also learning Urdu or English at school. That’s why your classroom might sound like a little mix of different places! It’s actually a wonderful thing. Different languages help people share their own stories, traditions, and ways of thinking.

If you’re ever curious about a classmate’s language, you can ask them nicely if they’d like to teach you a word or two. Many kids love sharing their home language with friends. And if you ever feel unsure about something you hear, it’s always okay to ask a teacher or a trusted adult to help explain it.

Does that make sense, or is there a specific word or sound you’ve been wondering about?
